panels.rationale: Peripheral blood smear from a patient with confirmed Bernard-Soulier syndrome shows moderate thrombocytopenia and large/giant platelets, with a green arrow marking a giant platelet. These are classic hematologic manifestations of BSS.
panels.attribution_text: Alasmari et al. A Novel Variant of GP9 Gene Resulting in Bernard-Soulier Syndrome: A Case Report.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.76363. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Peripheral blood smear x 100 with Wright-Giemsa staining showing moderate thrombocytopenia with occasional large and giant platelets (green arrow), and a manual platelet count of 70 x109/L.
in_text_mentions: PBS revealed giant platelets, as shown in Figure 1. Platelet function testing supported a diagnosis of BSS, with specific platelet membrane glycoprotein demonstrating elevated expression of CD61 (GpIIIa) and CD41 (GpIIB). Conversely, there was an absence of expression for CD42a (GPIX) and CD42B (GpIb). These findings are consistent with BSS. WES showed a GP9 gene mutation, confirming a diagnosis of BSS type c, as shown in Figure 2. Both parents were carriers of the same GP9 gene mutation. The patient received follow-up in our pediatric hematology clinic; her last platelet count was 160 × 109/L

plate_findings.evidence: Caption: 'Blood smear from a BSS patient showing the presence of macro platelets and a giant platelet (arrow)'

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Peripheral blood smear explicitly attributed to a Bernard-Soulier syndrome patient, with an arrow pointing to a giant platelet among red cells; macrothrombocytes are a hallmark laboratory finding of BSS. B: Second blood-smear field from the same BSS patient, showing platelets that are large relative to red cells with arrow annotations; consistent with the macrothrombocytosis characteristic of Bernard-Soulier syndrome.
panels.attribution_text: Lfaquir et al. Bernard-Soulier Syndrome: Case Studies From Morocco.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.87578. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Blood smear from a BSS patient showing the presence of macro platelets and a giant platelet (arrow) (x1000) BSS: Bernard-Soulier syndrome
in_text_mentions: Biologically, all patients had normal hemostasis parameters. Microcytic hypochromic anemia was observed in four cases. All showed thrombocytopenia except for one case in which thrombocytosis was observed in an 87-year-old patient. Blood smears from all patients revealed the presence of macroplatelets (Figure 1).

plate_findings.evidence: Caption: 'Abnormally large and irregularly shaped platelets seen in the preoperative microscopic examination'

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Peripheral blood smear panel of a patient diagnosed with Bernard-Soulier syndrome showing a markedly enlarged, irregularly shaped platelet among red cells, directly matching the captioned giant platelet finding. B: Blood smear field from the same patient showing a giant, irregular platelet far larger than surrounding erythrocytes, a hallmark of Bernard-Soulier syndrome. C: Blood smear field showing an abnormally large irregular platelet among red blood cells, consistent with the captioned Bernard-Soulier syndrome morphology. D: Additional blood smear field from the patient demonstrating a large, irregularly shaped platelet diagnostic of Bernard-Soulier syndrome giant platelets.
panels.attribution_text: Goncalves and Fortunato. Perioperative Management of a Frail Patient With Bernard-Soulier Syndrome. Cureus None. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Abnormally large and irregularly shaped platelets seen in the preoperative microscopic examination Peripheral blood smear was carried out with Sysmex SP-50 and the photograph digitized with Sysmex DI-60 (Sysmex, Kobe, Japan).
in_text_mentions: Preoperative investigations showed a hemoglobin level of 13 g/dL, platelet count of 30 x 109/L (normal range: 150-450 x 109/L), a normal coagulation profile, and an abnormal peripheral blood smear displaying abnormally large and irregularly shaped platelets (Figure 1). The high bleeding risk required multidisciplinary collaboration among immunohematology specialists, surgeons, and anesthesiologists.
